evidence.claim: Laurel was founded in October 1999; its 2002 company fact sheet names Atul Bansal as President and CEO, describes early commercial deployment in 2002, and names a multi-region service-provider market.
evidence.why: Clarifies that the Laurel identity/title timeline changes across dated official pages; validates commercial operating context rather than generic founder status.
evidence.source: Laurel Networks fact sheet, archived official page

evidence.claim: Laurel’s 2002 archived board page lists Atul Bansal as co-founder, CEO and President; it names Peter Barris (NEA), John Boyle (Worldview observer), Rob Coneybeer (NEA), Stephen Vogelsang, and Paul Vabakos (Trinity) in formal board/company context.
evidence.why: Upgrades the capital map from company-level funding to named, dated governance relationships. It does not prove current access or personal closeness.
evidence.source: Laurel Networks board page, archived official page

evidence.claim: Laurel’s official investor page says the company had nearly $90m from NEA, Trinity, Worldview, WorldCom Ventures, Rein Capital, and CommVest at that point; a later ECI release reports $118m from NEA, Trinity, and Ciena.
evidence.why: Explains the apparent funding discrepancy as a date/scope change, not a contradiction; Ciena appears in later acquirer disclosures, while the earlier official list shows a broader venture stack.
evidence.source: Laurel Networks investor page, archived official page

evidence.claim: Laurel’s technical-leadership page identifies Robert Rennison, Dimitris Varotsis, Jeffrey Prem, and Pat Duegaw as technical/operational leaders, all with FORE Systems or adjacent carrier-networking lineage.
evidence.why: Shows that Laurel was built from a repeatable FORE Systems talent cluster—not solely a lone-founder story. It identifies former colleague nodes, not guaranteed current relationships.
evidence.source: Laurel Networks technical leadership page, archived official page

evidence.claim: Laurel’s April 2005 newsletter documents the final pre-sale commercial posture: carrier automation/security features, a Grande Communications FTTH deployment, and a Telindus UK reseller agreement supporting European distribution.
evidence.why: Materially deepens the operating story immediately before acquisition: repeatable service-provider workflow, security/provisioning, a named customer deployment, and channel expansion.
evidence.source: Laurel Networks newsletter, archived official page

evidence.claim: ECI completed the purchase of 100% of Laurel in June 2005 for $88m cash and made it the Data Networking Division; ECI described the strategic rationale as adding edge routing/IP service capabilities to its broadband, optical, and core portfolio.
evidence.why: Primary transaction ground truth; supports one documented founder exit, not personal proceeds.
evidence.source: ECI Telecom acquisition release filed with SEC

evidence.claim: ECI’s 2006 annual filing reports that the acquired Data Networking Division registered a $19.6m operating loss from acquisition through 31 Dec 2005, with $37.1m allocated to Laurel goodwill.
evidence.why: Adds necessary exit forensic context: the sale created a strategic platform but ECI disclosed early integration/economic risk. It cannot be attributed to Atul personally or used as a verdict on the business.

evidence.claim: ECI’s 2007 annual filing says the former Data Networking Division recorded a $40.7m operating loss in 2006 versus $19.6m in the partial 2005 period. In January 2007 ECI merged it with Optical Networks into Transport Networking, retaining the IP routing technology; the filing reports $11.1m 2006 Data Networking sales.
evidence.why: Completes the exit forensic arc: technology was retained and incorporated into a broader platform despite commercial pressure. The filing does not allocate responsibility to Atul or establish his post-2005 employment duration.

evidence.claim: An official TimeSys appointment release says Atul Bansal became CEO on 10 April 2007, succeeding interim CEO Joseph Raffa, who became board chairman; it quotes Joel Adams, then Adams Capital general partner, on the board’s selection.
evidence.why: Explains the Laurel-to-Timesys transition as a board-led CEO recruitment, with direct historical investor-governance context.

evidence.claim: A source-dated Timesys management biography reports: B.S. Chemical Engineering, IIT Kanpur (1984); M.S. Chemical Engineering, University of Rhode Island (1987); M.S. Computer Science, University of Rhode Island (1989). It also states he became COO of ECI’s Data Networking Division after the Laurel acquisition and joined Timesys as CEO in 2007.
evidence.why: Fills professionally relevant education and post-exit operating links, but the undated/stale biography cannot establish any current board, India-LLP, advisory, or 2026 employment claim.
evidence.date: live page checked 13 Aug 2026; biographical content undated
evidence.confidence: MEDIUM-HIGH for historical biography; LOW for current status

evidence.claim: Lynx announced its acquisition of Timesys on 12 Dec 2023. It said the combined platform would pair Lynx’s mission-critical edge software with Timesys’s Linux development tools, cybersecurity solutions, and engineering services; CEO ally was exclusive M&A adviser.
evidence.why: Defines the second transaction as a business sale during Atul’s CEO tenure—not a second founder exit—and identifies the formal M&A path.

evidence.claim: A Lynx release with body dateline 13 Nov 2024 quotes Atul Bansal as “Lynx vice president of open-source business development” on embedded vulnerability management and SBOM lifecycle work.
evidence.why: Best official post-sale role signal; it is source-dated evidence, not proof of present 2026 employment.
evidence.date: 13 November 2024 body dateline; page date 11 February 2025
evidence.confidence: HIGH for source wording; LOW for current job status

evidence.claim: OceanSound’s corresponding acquisition announcement says over 200 customers across aerospace, defense, industrial, medical, and enterprise end markets relied on Timesys; it describes SBOM/SCA and managed lifecycle offerings.
evidence.why: Shows the industry environment Atul sold into and strengthens SARVAX fit only around governance, lifecycle discipline, and trusted execution—not financial-services buyer access.

evidence.why: This is the core strategic identity, supported by multiple independently dated company and transaction sources. It is not a claim of current employment or an AI/wealth-management investing thesis.
